questions.prompt: Put these five stages of the Oracle Fusion Assets lifecycle, per Lesson 1, in the order an asset actually moves through them.
items: Addition — the asset is recorded for the first time, manually, through Quick Additions, or via Mass Additions from a Payables invoice
Capitalization / placed in service — a construction-in-process asset is converted to depreciable status and its depreciation clock starts
Depreciation — each period, cost is recognized as expense based on the asset's method, life, and prorate convention
Adjustments and transfers — cost corrections, reclassifications, revaluations, impairments, and transfers happen while the asset is in service
Retirement — the asset is sold, scrapped, or otherwise taken out of service, triggering a gain or loss calculation
questions.explain: Every asset moves through the same five stages: it's added, then capitalized and placed in service (which is what actually starts the depreciation clock), then depreciates period after period while absorbing whatever adjustments and transfers happen along the way, and finally retires — triggering the gain/loss calculation that closes out its life on the books.

questions.prompt: Match each book-related term to what it actually is, per Lesson 3.
right: A secondary book, populated from a corporate book, used for tax reporting with potentially different depreciation rules
The process that copies asset additions and transactions from a corporate book into an associated tax book
The primary book, used for financial statement reporting under the company's primary accounting standard
Used to forecast and plan future depreciation and capital spending without affecting actual financial or tax books
questions.explain: The corporate book is the primary book for financial statement reporting. A tax book is a secondary book populated from a corporate book, with its own depreciation rules. A budget book forecasts future depreciation without touching actual books at all. Mass copy is the process that keeps a tax book synchronized with its corporate book.

questions.prompt: Meridian Fabrication Co.'s "Machinery" category is assigned a 10-year straight-line life in its corporate book and a 7-year 200% declining-balance method in its tax book. A new CNC machine is added to both books under this same category. What happens, and why?
options: The machine depreciates differently in each book, because a category's default depreciation rules are configured per category book — the combination of the category and a specific book — not once for the category company-wide.
The machine depreciates identically in both books, because once a category is created, its depreciation rules are fixed company-wide and can't vary by book.
The machine depreciates differently, but only because the tax book's recorded cost for the machine is different from the corporate book's cost.
This configuration is invalid — Oracle Fusion Assets requires every book to use the same depreciation method for a given category.
questions.explain: A category isn't configured once for the whole company — it's configured once per asset book, and that combination is called a category book. The category book, not the category itself, carries the default depreciation method, life, and convention, which is exactly why the same "Machinery" category can legitimately depreciate on a 10-year straight-line basis in the corporate book and a 7-year declining-balance basis in the tax book.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a company that already answers every location and property-tax question with its location flexfield, but also needs to track which assets were funded by a specific capital project or grant, would turn on the ________ flexfield to capture that, per Lesson 5.
questions.explain: The asset key flexfield is an optional, separate segment structure used to identify or group assets by something other than category or location — commonly a project, cost center, or grant code that neither of those other structures is built to answer.

questions.code:
Cost: $90,000
Salvage value: $10,000
Useful life: 8 years
questions.prompt: Using the straight-line formula from Lesson 6, what is the steady-state annual depreciation for this asset, before any first-year proration?
questions.explain: Annual depreciation = (Cost - Salvage Value) / Useful Life = ($90,000 - $10,000) / 8 = $10,000. $11,250 comes from dividing cost alone by life, forgetting to subtract salvage value first. $12,500 comes from adding salvage value to cost instead of subtracting it. $8,889 comes from dividing the correct $80,000 depreciable basis by the wrong life (9 years instead of 8).

questions.code:
Full-year straight-line depreciation: $12,000
Date placed in service: May 10
Fiscal year: calendar year (Jan-Dec)
Prorate convention: mid-month
questions.prompt: Under a mid-month prorate convention, what is this asset's year-one depreciation?
questions.explain: Mid-month treats an asset placed in service anywhere within a month as if it were placed in service at that month's midpoint, so May counts as a full month. Months remaining from May through December is 8 of 12: $12,000 x (8/12) = $8,000. $7,000 comes from miscounting the remaining months as 7 (wrongly excluding May itself). $6,000 is what a half-year convention would give instead (half of the annual amount, regardless of month). $12,000 is the full, unprorated annual amount.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about a depreciation book's period status, per Lesson 8.
options: At any moment, a depreciation book has exactly one period marked as the current open period.
Once a period closes, it generally cannot be reopened — the depreciation calendar only moves forward.
A book can run depreciation into any future period at any time, regardless of which period is currently open.
A mistake discovered after a period closes is typically fixed with a correcting transaction dated into the current open period, not by reopening the closed period.
The depreciation calendar and the General Ledger's accounting calendar must always use identical period names and boundaries.
questions.explain: A book always has exactly one current open period, and depreciation can only calculate into that period — never a future one, which rules out option C. Once closed, a period generally stays closed, so corrections go in as a dated transaction in the current open period rather than reopening history. The depreciation calendar is technically independent of the GL calendar; many implementations align them for easier reconciliation, but nothing requires it, which rules out option E.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: Oracle Fusion Assets stores an asset's useful life internally in ________ rather than whole years, so a "5-year life" is actually stored as 60.
questions.explain: Life in months is how Oracle Fusion Assets stores useful life internally, for precision below whole years — a 5-year life is stored as 60 months, which also makes a life like 7.5 years representable without a fractional year field.

questions.prompt: Meridian Fabrication Co. adds a new machine to its corporate book, which is associated with a tax book via mass copy. The corporate book uses a 10-year straight-line method for this category; the tax book uses a 7-year table-based method for the same category. Which statement correctly describes what happens?
options: Mass copy creates the same asset in the tax book, but the tax book's own category book record determines the 7-year table-based method there, not the corporate book's rules.

Mass copy creates the same asset in the tax book, and the tax book automatically depreciates it using the corporate book's 10-year straight-line method, since mass copy carries the depreciation method along with the cost and date placed in service.

Mass copy only copies the asset's cost and date placed in service into the tax book; someone must then manually re-enter the depreciation method, life, and prorate convention for every single asset before it can depreciate.
The asset isn't copied into the tax book automatically at all — someone has to run a separate, manual tax book addition for every asset that needs to exist in both books.
Mass copy changes the corporate book's depreciation method to match the tax book's method, so both books end up depreciating the asset the same way going forward.
Mass copy only runs one time, at implementation, so any asset added afterward in the corporate book will never appear in the associated tax book at all.
questions.explain: Mass copy copies the asset's existence, cost, and date placed in service from the corporate book into the associated tax book — but the tax book's own category book record, configured independently per Lesson 9, is what actually determines the depreciation method, life, and convention used there. That's exactly why the same real asset can depreciate on two different schedules in the two books.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the closest wrong answer because it correctly describes mass copy carrying the asset's existence, cost, and date placed in service into the tax book — but it gets backwards which book's rules govern depreciation there. Mass copy doesn't drag the corporate book's depreciation method along with it; the tax book's own category book record governs depreciation in the tax book, which is the entire point of configuring category books per book instead of once per company.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of turning a Payables invoice into a posted, depreciating asset in the correct order, per Lessons 13-15.
items: A Payables invoice distribution is coded to an asset clearing account rather than an expense account
Create Mass Additions sends the eligible distribution into the Fixed Assets interface table as a new mass addition line
Prepare Mass Additions reviews the line, setting its category and marking it POST (after merging or splitting it first if needed)
Post Mass Additions creates a new asset number, or a cost adjustment on an existing asset, and changes the line's status to POSTED
The asset begins accumulating depreciation starting from its date placed in service
questions.explain: An invoice only becomes mass-addition-eligible once it's coded to an asset clearing account. Create Mass Additions then moves it into the Fixed Assets interface table as a candidate, not yet a real asset. Prepare Mass Additions is where a person reviews, categorizes, and marks it POST. Post Mass Additions is the actual boundary where it becomes a real asset number or cost adjustment. Only after posting does depreciation start accumulating, from the date placed in service.

questions.prompt: Meridian buys twelve identical laptops at $1,400 each for its sales team, all placed in service the same day in the well-established "Computer Equipment / Laptops" category — except three of the twelve need to charge a different cost center than the other nine, starting immediately. Why does this force those three laptops out of Quick Additions?
options: Quick Additions has no way to split a single addition across multiple distributions — any asset that needs a non-default distribution from the moment it's added requires the full manual Add Asset flow instead.
Quick Additions can only be used for assets costing under $1,000, so these $1,400 laptops were never eligible for it in the first place.
Quick Additions requires every asset in a batch to go to the same category, and a different cost center automatically means a different category.
Quick Additions doesn't support assets with more than one unit, so twelve identical laptops can never be added together through it.
questions.explain: Quick Additions is deliberately stripped down and has no screen for setting up multiple distributions at the point of addition — that's exactly one of the cases Lesson 12 lists where Quick Additions is the wrong tool, forcing a return to the full Add Asset flow from Lesson 11.

questions.prompt: A $90,000 mass addition line described as "3 forklifts, Model FX-200" arrives in Prepare Mass Additions. Select every true statement about correctly preparing this line, per Lesson 14.
options: The line needs to be split into three separate lines of $30,000 each before each forklift can be posted as its own asset with its own number.
If Meridian already owned one of these exact forklifts and this invoice was actually a follow-up cost for it, the line should be merged into the existing asset instead of split into new ones.
A mass addition line's queue status is fixed the moment Create Mass Additions runs, and can't be changed during Prepare Mass Additions.
If the category on the line is blank or incorrect, Prepare Mass Additions is where it gets set or corrected before posting.
Splitting a line into multiple lines changes the total dollar amount being added, since each new split line gets the category's default cost instead of a share of the original invoice amount.
questions.explain: A line covering three physical assets in one dollar amount needs to be split so each forklift becomes its own asset. A line that's actually additional cost on an asset Meridian already owns should be merged, not split into new assets. Category correction is exactly what the review step is for. The queue status is not fixed at arrival — NEW, ON HOLD, POST, MERGED, SPLIT, and DELETE are all set and changed during Prepare Mass Additions. Splitting a line divides its original dollar amount proportionally across the new lines; it doesn't replace that amount with category defaults.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a construction-in-process asset's depreciation clock starts on its date placed in service, set when the asset is ________ — not on the date its first invoice arrived, and not on the date it was first added to the system as CIP.
questions.explain: Capitalizing a CIP asset is the action that converts it from CIP to a regular, depreciable asset and sets its date placed in service — the date depreciation actually starts, independent of when the underlying construction costs were originally invoiced.

questions.code:
CIP asset accumulates $360,000 across invoices from February through May.
Capitalized with date placed in service: June 1.
Category: 15-year straight-line life, no salvage value.
questions.prompt: What is the correct full annual depreciation once this asset is past its first partial year, and how much depreciation applies to February through May?
options: $24,000 per year ($360,000 / 15); $0 for February through May, since a CIP asset doesn't depreciate until it's capitalized.
$24,000 per year; some partial depreciation for February through May as well, prorated based on when each invoice posted.
$360,000 / 4 months = $90,000 depreciated across February-May, then $24,000 per year afterward.
$24,000 per year, applied retroactively starting in February, since that's when cost first began accumulating on the asset.
questions.explain: $360,000 / 15 = $24,000 per year once the asset is past its first partial year. A CIP asset never depreciates while it's CIP, no matter how much cost has accumulated or how long it's been sitting there — so February through May, before capitalization, gets exactly $0 regardless of the four months of invoices that landed on it.

questions.prompt: Meridian runs Calculate Depreciation in preview mode for its corporate book, and the exception report shows two assets failed: one with a missing depreciation expense account, one with a category that was deleted after the asset was added. What has to happen before Meridian can successfully close the period?
options: The underlying data problems on both assets need to be fixed — a valid depreciation expense account and a valid category — then depreciation needs to be rerun before the period can close, since a period generally cannot close while assets have failed to depreciate.
Nothing — preview mode doesn't actually affect whether the period can close, so Meridian can run final mode immediately regardless of the exception report.
The two failed assets need to be retired so they no longer count toward the period's depreciation run.
Meridian should roll back depreciation for the entire book, since any single asset's failure in preview mode invalidates the whole run.
questions.explain: An asset failing to depreciate because of a data problem — a missing account, a deleted category — is exactly the hard stop Lesson 17 describes: a period generally cannot close while any assets have failed to depreciate. The fix is correcting the underlying data, not retiring the asset or rolling back a run that was only ever in preview mode and never committed anything in the first place.

questions.prompt: Meridian's machine was set up with a 10-year straight-line life ($10,000/year) but should have been 8 years ($12,500/year) all along. Two years in, $20,000 has been taken, but $25,000 should have been taken at the corrected rate — a $5,000 shortfall. Which statement correctly distinguishes an amortized adjustment from an expensed adjustment for this $5,000?
options: An expensed adjustment recognizes the full $5,000 in the current period all at once; an amortized adjustment instead spreads that $5,000 across the asset's remaining 6 years, smoothing the correction into future periods.

An amortized adjustment recognizes the full $5,000 in the current period all at once; an expensed adjustment instead spreads that $5,000 across the asset's remaining 6 years, smoothing the correction into future periods.
Both an amortized and an expensed adjustment recognize the $5,000 immediately — the only real difference between them is which GL account the catch-up amount posts to.
An expensed adjustment reduces the asset's remaining life by one year to absorb the shortfall, while an amortized adjustment extends its remaining life by one year instead.

An expensed adjustment recognizes the full $5,000 in the current period; an amortized adjustment spreads it across the asset's entire original 8-year life, including the two years that have already closed.
Neither adjustment type actually changes recognized depreciation expense — both simply update the asset's life field going forward with no catch-up amount recognized at all.
questions.explain: An expensed adjustment hits the entire $5,000 catch-up in the current period all at once, as a visible bump. An amortized adjustment instead spreads that same $5,000 across the asset's remaining 6 years of life, adding a smaller amount on top of the new $12,500/year rate each year going forward instead of front-loading it.
questions.distractorExplain: Option B is the exact reverse of the correct mapping — it swaps which adjustment type front-loads the catch-up into the current period and which one smooths it across future periods, which is precisely the mix-up this lesson warns against. Option E is also tempting because it keeps the correct idea that an amortized adjustment spreads the catch-up rather than expensing it immediately, but it gets the span wrong: it spreads across the 6 years of life still remaining, not the entire original 8-year life including the two years that are already closed and can no longer be adjusted.

questions.code:
Original: $120,000 cost, $20,000 salvage, 10-year life, straight-line ($10,000/year)
Cost adjustment: +$15,000 for a late installation invoice, 6 months after the original addition
questions.prompt: What is the new annual depreciation rate on the corrected cost, and why does this adjustment likely trigger at least some catch-up depreciation?
options: ($135,000 - $20,000) / 10 = $11,500/year; since depreciation had already been running at the lower $10,000/year rate before the cost increase was recorded, the periods since the original addition were under-depreciated relative to the corrected basis.
($135,000 - $20,000) / 10 = $11,500/year; no catch-up is possible, because cost adjustments only ever apply going forward from the date they're entered.
$135,000 / 10 = $13,500/year, ignoring salvage value since the adjustment is for an installation cost rather than the machine itself.
The depreciation rate stays $10,000/year, because a cost adjustment only affects an asset's net book value, not its depreciable basis.
questions.explain: The depreciable basis grows to $135,000 - $20,000 = $115,000, over 10 years = $11,500/year. Because the asset had already been depreciating at the old $10,000/year rate for six months before this correction was recorded, those six months took less depreciation than the corrected basis says they should have — exactly the catch-up problem Lesson 18 describes, just triggered by a cost change instead of a life change.

questions.prompt: Match each transaction type to what it actually is.
right: Formally restating an asset's carrying value to reflect current conditions, not correcting an original error, using a reserve and amortization account
Changing an asset's category, with cost and (usually) location unchanged — can still trigger catch-up depreciation
An indicator-driven write-down to an asset's recoverable amount when it falls below carrying value, triggered by an unplanned adverse event
Correcting or changing the recorded dollar amount of an asset's cost, with category and location unchanged
questions.explain: A cost adjustment corrects the dollar amount only. A reclassification corrects the category only, which can still change the depreciation rate and trigger a catch-up even though nothing physically changed. A revaluation restates value under a specific accounting policy, using a reserve and amortization account rather than correcting an error. An impairment is an unplanned, indicator-driven write-down when an asset's recoverable amount falls below its carrying value.

questions.code:
Building net book value: $400,000
Remaining life: 20 years
Revalued fair value: $500,000
questions.prompt: After this revaluation, what is the new annual depreciation, and what happens to the $100,000 increase?
options: $500,000 / 20 = $25,000/year going forward; the $100,000 increase is recorded in a revaluation reserve, typically in equity, not as immediate income.
$400,000 / 20 = $20,000/year continues unchanged; the $100,000 increase is simply ignored unless the asset is later sold.
$500,000 / 20 = $25,000/year going forward; the $100,000 increase is recognized immediately as a one-time gain on the income statement.
$600,000 / 20 = $30,000/year, since the $100,000 increase is added on top of the new $500,000 fair value rather than replacing the old basis.
questions.explain: Once revalued, depreciation is based on the new, revalued amount: $500,000 / 20 years = $25,000/year. The $100,000 increase goes to a revaluation reserve, typically recorded in equity rather than flowing through the income statement immediately — keeping the revaluation surplus distinguishable from ordinary depreciation expense.

questions.code:
Packaging line carrying amount (net book value): $280,000
Recoverable amount (higher of fair value less costs to sell, or value in use): $190,000
questions.prompt: What is the impairment loss, and what happens to future depreciation on this asset?
options: Impairment loss = $280,000 - $190,000 = $90,000, recognized as an expense; future depreciation recalculates on the new $190,000 basis over the asset's remaining useful life.
Impairment loss = $280,000 - $190,000 = $90,000, but future depreciation keeps calculating on the original $280,000 basis, since impairment only affects the current period's expense.
Impairment loss = $190,000 - $280,000 = -$90,000, meaning this is actually a gain, not a loss, since the recoverable amount is lower.
No impairment loss applies unless the asset is already fully depreciated down to zero.
questions.explain: An asset is impaired when its recoverable amount is less than its carrying amount. The impairment loss is carrying amount minus recoverable amount: $280,000 - $190,000 = $90,000, recognized as an expense. Depreciation going forward is recalculated on the new, lower $190,000 basis over the remaining useful life — a permanently lower depreciation charge than before the impairment.

questions.prompt: Match each kind of transfer to what it actually changes, per Lesson 23.
right: Reassigning an asset to a different employee or custodian, without necessarily moving it physically
Changing which cost center or expense account bears an asset's depreciation expense
Updating an asset's location flexfield to reflect where it physically moved
questions.explain: A location transfer updates where the asset physically sits. An assignment transfer reassigns who's responsible for it, with no required physical move. A distribution transfer changes which cost center bears its depreciation expense. All three can apply to the same real-world event, and none of them touch the asset's cost or category.

questions.prompt: Meridian moves a CNC machine from its Ohio plant to its Texas plant, reassigns it to a new supervisor, and shifts its depreciation expense from the Ohio cost center to the Texas cost center — with no change to the machine's cost or category. What kind of transaction is this, and why isn't it a reclassification?
options: It's a transfer — specifically all three types (location, assignment, and distribution) at once — because reclassification is specifically about correcting which category an asset belongs to, and this asset's category never changed.
It's a reclassification, because three separate things about the asset are changing at once, and reclassification is defined by how many fields change in a single transaction.
It's a cost adjustment, because moving an asset between plants changes its depreciable basis.
It can only be one of the three transfer types at a time — Oracle Fusion Assets doesn't allow location, assignment, and distribution transfers to be combined in a single real-world event.
questions.explain: A transfer moves an asset's "where," not its "what." This single real-world event touches all three transfer types at once, but the machine's category and cost never change, which is exactly what keeps it from being a reclassification — reclassification is specifically about the category being wrong, not about how many things happen to change together.

questions.code:
Delivery van: $45,000 original cost, fully depreciated to $0 net book value
Sold for scrap: $1,200 proceeds, $0 cost of removal
questions.prompt: What is the gain or loss on this retirement?
options: $1,200 gain — Gain/Loss = Proceeds - Cost of removal - Net book value = $1,200 - $0 - $0 = $1,200, and since net book value is already zero, the entire proceeds amount becomes a gain.
$0 — a fully depreciated asset can never generate a gain or loss on retirement, regardless of proceeds received.
$43,800 loss — the gain/loss formula should subtract the proceeds from the original cost, not from the net book value.
$1,200 loss, because any amount received for an asset that's already fully depreciated must be recorded as a loss rather than a gain.
questions.explain: The gain/loss formula is Proceeds of Sale minus Cost of Removal minus Net Book Value. With net book value already at zero, there's nothing left to offset the proceeds against, so the entire $1,200 becomes a gain: $1,200 - $0 - $0 = $1,200.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank with a number: Meridian's 20-unit shelving asset ($500/unit, $10,000 total) has 5 units damaged and scrapped. Retiring by units, Oracle Fusion Assets calculates $________ of cost being retired.
questions.explain: Retiring by units lets Oracle Fusion Assets calculate the proportional cost automatically: 5 of the 20 units, at $500 each, is 5/20 x $10,000 = $2,500 of cost retired, leaving $7,500 of cost on the remaining 15 units.

questions.prompt: Meridian retires a CNC machine by mistake — the wrong asset number was selected during a mass retirement upload — and the error is caught the same week, before period close. What's the correct fix, and why is simply adding the machine back as a new asset addition the wrong approach?
options: Reinstate the retirement, which restores the original asset's status, its original date placed in service, and its accumulated depreciation history — a new addition would start a brand-new depreciation schedule with no connection to the asset's prior history.
Add the machine back as a new asset addition, since that's the only way to restore it to in-service status once it's been retired at all.
Reinstatement and a new addition produce identical results, so either approach is equally correct as long as the asset ends up back in service.
Reinstate the retirement, but only after the period closes and accounting has been created and transferred — reinstating before that point isn't allowed.
questions.explain: Reinstatement reverses an erroneous retirement, restoring the asset's original identity, date placed in service, and accumulated depreciation history. A new addition would instead start a fresh depreciation schedule with no connection to the asset's prior life — and reinstatement is actually time-limited to before the retirement's accounting is created and the period closes, the opposite of option D's claim.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of Fixed Assets period close in the correct order, per Lesson 32.
items: Finish transaction entry — every addition, adjustment, transfer, and retirement for the period is entered and posted
Run depreciation in preview mode and review the exception report for assets that failed to depreciate
Run depreciation in final mode, which commits the period's depreciation and closes the current period
Run Create Accounting in final mode to generate journal entries for the period's transactions and depreciation
Transfer the journal entries to the General Ledger as a journal batch
Reconcile Assets' balances against GL's posted balances for every fixed-asset account
questions.explain: Each step depends on the one before it: transaction entry has to be complete before depreciation runs, preview has to look clean before committing to final, Create Accounting needs a committed depreciation run to generate entries from, GL transfer needs those entries to exist first, and reconciliation is the final check that everything agrees once it's all posted.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about the Fixed Assets to General Ledger transfer process, per Lesson 29.
options: Transfer moves journal entry data from Assets into GL as an unposted journal batch; it doesn't by itself update GL account balances.
Post is the separate General Ledger action that actually updates account balances based on a journal batch.
Transfer and post always happen in the exact same automatic step, so there's never a batch sitting in GL that's transferred but not yet posted.
How often Fixed Assets transfers to GL — every transaction, daily, or only at period end — is a deliberate tradeoff, not a universally "correct" setting.
If Assets and GL don't agree on a fixed-asset account balance, the most likely explanation is always a configuration error in the category book's account mapping.
questions.explain: Transfer and post are two distinct actions: transfer moves data into GL as an unposted batch, and post is the separate step that updates balances — they can happen at different times, which is exactly why option C is wrong. Transfer frequency is a genuine tradeoff between currency and processing overhead, not a fixed rule. And the most common cause of an apparent imbalance is timing (a batch not yet transferred or posted), not account mapping, which rules out option E.

questions.prompt: Meridian's accumulated depreciation account doesn't reconcile between the Assets reserve ledger and the General Ledger for the current period. Per Lesson 31, which cause should be investigated first, and why?
options: Timing — check whether a batch is sitting accounted in Assets but not yet transferred, or transferred but not yet posted in GL — since this is the most common cause and is fastest to rule out before investigating anything else.
A manual GL entry bypassing Assets — this should always be checked first, since it's the single most common cause of an out-of-balance condition in every implementation.
An incorrect account mapping in a category book — this should be checked first, since it's the hardest problem to fix and therefore needs the most lead time.
A failed Create Accounting run — this should be checked first, because timing-related gaps between Assets and GL are actually rare in practice.
questions.explain: Lesson 31 lists timing as the most common cause of an apparent imbalance and the fastest to check: a batch simply hasn't finished moving through transfer and post yet, which looks like a discrepancy but resolves itself once the batch catches up. Only after ruling that out does it make sense to dig into a manual GL bypass, a failed Create Accounting run, or an account mapping error.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: like depreciation runs, Create Accounting can run in draft mode for review, or in ________ mode, which commits the entries and makes them eligible to transfer to the General Ledger.
questions.explain: Draft mode generates journal entries for review without committing anything. Final mode commits those entries, making them eligible for the Fixed Assets to General Ledger transfer covered in Lesson 29.

questions.prompt: Meridian's controller needs to know whether every mass addition from last month actually finished posting, and separately wants to see every construction-in-process asset still sitting uncapitalized. Which two reports answer these, respectively?
options: Asset additions report for the first question; CIP report for the second.
Reserve ledger report for the first question; depreciation projection report for the second.
Fully reserved assets report for the first question; asset cost detail report for the second.
Retirements report for the first question; asset additions report for the second.
questions.explain: The asset additions report lists every asset added in a period, exactly what's needed to confirm last month's mass additions all posted. The CIP report lists every asset still sitting in construction-in-process status, uncapitalized — exactly the population the controller's second question is asking about.
